print_output.notes: Printing variables, expressions (print(2 + 3) vs print('2 + 3')) and f-strings are left to B02 variables/expressions and B03 string_formatting; they should encompass these topics. Quotes inside strings and escaping quotes are left to B03 strings; only \n and \t are taught here because output layout needs them.

running_scripts.notes: statements_run_in_order is environment-agnostic (works in a browser IDE) so it can be core; run_from_terminal is the local-install path. Full traceback reading belongs to B09 debugging/exceptions.

comments.notes: Docstrings are B05; pseudocode-as-comments is B05 pseudocode.

command_line.notes: Only what a Python learner needs (navigation, paths, file management). Linux filesystem, permissions, redirection are out of scope per plan.json. Command-line arguments to scripts are B10 command_line_args.

python_setup.notes: pip and virtual environments belong to tool_pip / third_party_packages in a later batch.

pep8_style.notes: Only layout rules applicable to wave-1 code. Naming conventions (snake_case, UPPER_CASE constants, CapWords classes) should be owned by B02 variables/constants, B05 functions and the OOP batch, encompassing pep8_style.spacing_and_layout.

computer_architecture.notes: Introduced by py4e only; one supplemental topic.

topics.title: Your first program: printing text
topics.summary: Write print("...") to display a line of text, use matching quotes, print blank lines, and recognise the typos that stop print from working.

knowledge_points.title: Print a line of text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hello, world!")
# Hello, world!
The text goes in quotes, inside the parentheses after print.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the exact output of one or two print calls; write the call that displays a given sentence.

knowledge_points.title: Single or double quotes, as long as they match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print('Hi there')
print("Hi there")
# Both print: Hi there
print('Hi there") is a SyntaxError: the quotes must match.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which of several print lines run and which are SyntaxErrors; fix a line with mismatched quotes.

knowledge_points.title: Each print starts a new line; print() alone prints a blank line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
print()
print("two")
# one
#
# two  (the middle line is empty)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict multi-line output including blank lines; reorder print lines (Parsons) to produce a target output.

knowledge_points.title: Typos that break print
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Print("hi")    # NameError: Python names are case-sensitive
print "hi"     # SyntaxError: missing parentheses
print("hi"     # SyntaxError: "(" was never closed
knowledge_points.practice: For each line say 'prints' or 'error' and which error; fix three broken print lines.

topics.title: Printing numbers and several values at once
topics.summary: Print numbers, and pass several comma-separated values to one print call, which separates them with a space.

knowledge_points.title: Printing numbers without quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(42)
print("42")
# 42
# 42
Numbers need no quotes; both lines look the same on screen.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of prints with numbers and quoted digits; spot which line is a number and which is text.

knowledge_points.title: Several values in one print, separated by a space
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hello", "Ada")
# Hello Ada
Each comma-separated value is printed with one space between.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of print calls with 2-4 arguments; write one print that matches a target line.

knowledge_points.title: Mixing text and numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Age:", 36)
print("Total", 3, "items")
# Age: 36
# Total 3 items
knowledge_points.practice: Write print calls that combine a label and a number; predict the exact spacing.

knowledge_points.title: A comma inside quotes vs between arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a,b")
print("a", "b")
# a,b
# a b
Inside quotes a comma is just text; outside it separates values.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of look-alike pairs; fix a print that shows a stray comma or misses a space.

topics.title: Controlling separators and line endings: sep and end
topics.summary: Use print's sep= and end= keyword arguments to change what goes between values and what is printed after them.

knowledge_points.title: sep changes the separator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("2026", "10", "12", sep="-")
# 2026-10-12
sep replaces the default single space.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for different sep values; write a print that produces a dash- or slash-joined line.

knowledge_points.title: sep="" glues values together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("snow", "man", sep="")
# snowman
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output with sep=""; fix a print that leaves an unwanted space between values.

knowledge_points.title: end changes what comes after the line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")
# Loading...done
The default end is a newline; replacing it keeps the next print on the same line.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the combined output of two or three prints using end; fill in the end= value to join two lines.

knowledge_points.title: Combining sep and end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a", "b", sep="+", end="=")
print("ab")
# a+b=ab
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of prints using both arguments; write a print matching a target exactly.

topics.title: Laying out output with \n and \t
topics.summary: Put line breaks and tabs inside a printed string with the escape sequences \n and \t to lay out multi-line output from a single print.

knowledge_points.title: \n starts a new line inside one string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Roses\nViolets")
# Roses
# Violets
Backslash-n is one character: a line break.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines a print with \n produces and what is on each.

knowledge_points.title: Several prints vs one print with \n
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a")
print("b")
print("a\nb")
# both produce a, then b on the next line
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite three print calls as one; decide which pairs of programs give identical output.

knowledge_points.title: \t lines text up in columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Name\tScore")
print("Ada\t9")
Tabs jump to the next tab stop, so short columns line up.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in escape sequences to build a two-column table; predict output containing tabs.

knowledge_points.title: Common slips: /n and blank lines
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hi/nthere")   # prints Hi/nthere: forward slash is not an escape
print("Hi\n")        # prints Hi then an empty line
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that use /n or produce an extra blank line; draw small text art from a single print.

topics.title: How a program runs: top to bottom, until an error
topics.summary: Predict what a program prints given that statements run in order, a SyntaxError stops everything before it starts, and a runtime error stops the program at that line; read the line number and error type in the message.

knowledge_points.title: Statements run top to bottom, one at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("first")
print("second")
print("third")
Output appears in exactly the order of the lines.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output order; reorder lines (Parsons) to print a target sequence.

knowledge_points.title: A SyntaxError means nothing runs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
print("two"
print("three")
No output at all: Python checks the whole file before running any of it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output (or none) for files containing a syntax error on various lines.

knowledge_points.title: A runtime error stops at its line; earlier lines already ran
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
Print("two")
print("three")
# one
# NameError on line 2; line 3 never runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines print before the error; contrast with the SyntaxError case.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the error message: line number and error type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 2, in <module>
    Print("two")
NameError: name 'Print' is not defined
The last line names the error; "line 2" says where to look.
knowledge_points.practice: Given an error message, give the line number and error type; fix the line it points to.

topics.title: Running a .py file from the terminal
topics.summary: Run a saved script with python3 file.py from the right folder, fix the 'can't open file' error, and re-run after editing.

knowledge_points.title: python3 hello.py runs the file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 hello.py
Hello, world!
The terminal runs every line of hello.py and shows its output.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the command that runs a named file; predict the terminal output for a given hello.py.

knowledge_points.title: You must be in the folder that holds the file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 hello.py
python3: can't open file '/Users/ada/hello.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory
$ cd projects
$ python3 hello.py
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose 'can't open file' from a pwd/ls transcript; write the cd that fixes it.

knowledge_points.title: Run a file in another folder by giving its path
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 projects/hello.py
The argument is a path, so relative and absolute paths both work.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the command that runs a file given the current folder and the file's location.

knowledge_points.title: Edit, save, re-run
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Change the file, save it, then press Up and Enter to repeat python3 hello.py.
An unsaved edit runs the old version.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when a change was or was not saved; order the edit-save-run steps.

topics.title: Writing comments with #
topics.summary: Add full-line and inline comments that Python ignores, tell comments apart from # inside text, and comment out a line to switch it off.

knowledge_points.title: A # line is ignored
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Greet the user
print("Hello")
Everything after # on a line is for humans; Python skips it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of programs containing comment lines.

knowledge_points.title: Inline comments after code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hi")  # says hi
Code before the # runs; the rest of the line is ignored.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output; fix a line where the comment swallowed part of the code.

knowledge_points.title: # inside quotes is text, not a comment
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("#1 fan")  # a real comment
# #1 fan
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of lines mixing # in strings and comments.

knowledge_points.title: Commenting out code to switch it off
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a")
# print("b")
print("c")
# a
# c
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which line to comment out to produce a target output; predict output after commenting out lines.

topics.title: Writing comments that help
topics.summary: Judge and write comments that explain why rather than restate the code, keep them in sync with the code, and span several lines correctly.

knowledge_points.title: Explain why, not what
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# print("Total:", 3)  restates the code: unhelpful
# Sandcastle needs 3 buckets per tower  explains the reason: helpful
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the most useful comment for a snippet; rewrite a 'what' comment as a 'why' comment.

knowledge_points.title: Out-of-date comments mislead
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Prints the price in euros
print("Price:", 5, "USD")
The comment and code disagree; fix one so they match.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the comment that no longer matches its code in a short program.

knowledge_points.title: Multi-line comments: one # per line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Step 1: greet the user
# Step 2: print the menu
print("Welcome")
Each comment line needs its own #.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a block where a continuation line lacks #; write a two-line plan as comments above code.

topics.title: The terminal: prompt, commands and moving between folders
topics.summary: Read a shell prompt, type commands with arguments, and use pwd, ls and cd to find out where you are and move between folders.

knowledge_points.title: Prompt, command, arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ ls -l projects
ls is the command, -l is an option (flag), projects is an argument. $ is the prompt: don't type it.
knowledge_points.practice: Label the command, options and arguments in several command lines.

knowledge_points.title: pwd and ls: where am I, what is here
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ pwd
/Users/ada
$ ls
Desktop  Documents  projects
knowledge_points.practice: Given a folder tree, predict pwd and ls output.

knowledge_points.title: cd into a folder and cd .. back out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ cd projects
$ pwd
/Users/ada/projects
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/Users/ada
knowledge_points.practice: Trace pwd through a sequence of cd commands; write the cd commands to reach a target folder.

knowledge_points.title: When cd fails
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ cd Projects
cd: no such file or directory: Projects
Names are case-sensitive on macOS/Linux, and cd only sees folders inside the current one.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether each cd succeeds from a given location; fix the failing command.

topics.title: Absolute and relative paths
topics.summary: Write absolute and relative paths, use ~, . and .., and quote paths containing spaces.

knowledge_points.title: Absolute paths start at the root
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ cd /Users/ada/projects
A path starting with / works from anywhere; one without / is relative to the current folder.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify paths as absolute or relative; predict the folder reached from a given starting point.

knowledge_points.title: Relative paths with folders and ..
knowledge_points.worked_example:
From /Users/ada/projects:
$ cd ../Documents/notes
$ pwd
/Users/ada/Documents/notes
knowledge_points.practice: Trace multi-step relative paths; write the relative path between two folders in a tree.

knowledge_points.title: ~ is home, . is here
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ cd ~/projects    # same as /Users/ada/projects
$ ls .            # list the current folder
knowledge_points.practice: Expand ~ paths to absolute paths; choose equivalent paths.

knowledge_points.title: Paths with spaces need quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ cd My Files      # fails: two arguments
$ cd "My Files"    # works
knowledge_points.practice: Fix commands that break on spaces in names.

topics.title: Creating, moving and deleting files in the terminal
topics.summary: Make folders and files, rename and move them with mv, delete them with rm (which has no undo), and save typing with Tab completion and history.

knowledge_points.title: mkdir makes a folder, a new file comes from the editor or touch
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ mkdir week1
$ cd week1
$ touch hello.py
$ ls
hello.py
knowledge_points.practice: Predict ls output after a sequence of mkdir/touch/cd commands.

knowledge_points.title: mv renames or moves
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ mv hello.py greet.py      # rename
$ mv greet.py ../archive/    # move into another folder
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the folder tree after mv commands; write the mv for a given rename or move.

knowledge_points.title: rm deletes for good
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ rm old.py
$ rm -r drafts      # whole folder
There is no trash and no undo; double-check before pressing Enter.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which command removes exactly the intended files; spot the dangerous command in a list.

knowledge_points.title: Tab completion and Up-arrow history
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Type cd pro then Tab to complete projects/; press Up to recall the previous command.
This avoids typos in long names.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the keystrokes that repeat a previous command; predict what Tab completes to in a given folder.

topics.title: Installing Python and checking the version
topics.summary: Install Python 3, confirm it from the terminal with a version command, read the version number, and diagnose 'command not found'.

knowledge_points.title: Check the version from the terminal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 --version
Python 3.12.4
On Windows the launcher is: py --version
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right version command for macOS/Linux and Windows; read a version from sample output.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a version number
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Python 3.12.4 means major 3, minor 12, patch 4.
Python 2.7 is a different, retired language version: code in this course needs 3.x.
knowledge_points.practice: Order versions from oldest to newest; decide whether a given version is new enough for a requirement.

knowledge_points.title: Install from python.org or a package manager
knowledge_points.worked_example: Download the installer from python.org (on Windows tick 'Add python.exe to PATH'), then open a NEW terminal and re-check the version.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the installation and verification steps.

knowledge_points.title: 'command not found' means not installed or not on PATH
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 --version
zsh: command not found: python3
The shell searches the folders in PATH; fix by installing or adding Python to PATH, then reopen the terminal.
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose sample error transcripts: not installed, wrong command name (python vs python3 vs py), or terminal not restarted.

topics.title: Which Python is running?
topics.summary: Find which Python installation the terminal and the editor are using, and fix 'works in one place but not the other' mismatches.

knowledge_points.title: Several Pythons can be installed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ which python3
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
On Windows: where python. The first match on PATH is the one that runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Given which/where output, decide which installation a command will run.

knowledge_points.title: The editor picks its own interpreter
knowledge_points.worked_example: VS Code shows the selected interpreter in the status bar (e.g. 3.12.4). If it differs from the terminal's python3, the two can behave differently.
knowledge_points.practice: Match symptoms to the cause 'editor and terminal use different interpreters'; choose the fix.

knowledge_points.title: Browser-based environments come with Python
knowledge_points.worked_example: cs50.dev, the Code in Place IDE and py4e's online shell already have Python installed; checking python3 --version there still works.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide for each scenario whether a local install is needed.

topics.title: The interactive interpreter (REPL)
topics.summary: Start the Python REPL, evaluate expressions at the >>> prompt, leave it, and tell the shell prompt and the Python prompt apart.

knowledge_points.title: Start the REPL
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3
Python 3.12.4 ...
>>>
The >>> prompt means Python is waiting for one line of code.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify which prompt ($ or >>>) a transcript is at; choose the command that starts the REPL.

knowledge_points.title: Values are echoed back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> 7
7
>>> 'hi'
'hi'
>>> print('hi')
hi
The REPL shows each value it evaluates.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what the REPL shows after each typed line.

knowledge_points.title: Leave with exit() or Ctrl-D
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> exit()
$
Ctrl-D (macOS/Linux) or Ctrl-Z then Enter (Windows) also quits.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose how to leave the REPL on each OS; order the keystrokes to start, run a line, and quit.

knowledge_points.title: Typing at the wrong prompt
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> python3 hello.py
SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Shell commands go at $, Python code at >>>.
knowledge_points.practice: For each transcript say which prompt the line belonged at; fix the session.

topics.title: REPL echo vs print in a script
topics.summary: Explain why the REPL shows quotes and a script shows nothing for a bare value, use print in scripts, and use help() in the REPL.

knowledge_points.title: Echo shows quotes, print shows text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> 'Ada'
'Ada'
>>> print('Ada')
Ada
The echo shows how Python writes the value; print shows the text itself.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict REPL output for echoed values vs printed values.

knowledge_points.title: A bare value in a script prints nothing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# hello.py
'Hello'
print('Bye')
$ python3 hello.py
Bye
Only the REPL echoes; scripts need print.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict script output; fix a script that 'prints nothing'.

knowledge_points.title: help() in the REPL
knowledge_points.worked_example:
>>> help(print)
Shows print's documentation, including sep and end; press q to leave.
knowledge_points.practice: Use help output to answer a question about print's default separator.

topics.title: Creating and saving a .py file in a code editor
topics.summary: Create a .py file in a code editor (not a word processor), save it in a known folder, and avoid curly-quote and unsaved-file bugs.

knowledge_points.title: A code editor, not a word processor
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(“Hi”)   # SyntaxError: invalid character '“'
Word processors turn quotes curly; code editors keep plain " quotes.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot lines with curly quotes or other pasted characters; fix them.

knowledge_points.title: Name the file with .py
knowledge_points.worked_example: hello.py is a Python file; hello.txt or hello.py.txt is not run as Python by the editor.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick valid Python file names; fix names that would not be recognised.

knowledge_points.title: Save before you run
knowledge_points.worked_example: A dot or circle on the tab means unsaved changes. Running now runs the last saved version.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when the visible code and the saved code differ.

knowledge_points.title: Know which folder the file is in
knowledge_points.worked_example: Open a folder (workspace) first, then create the file inside it, so the terminal can find it later.
knowledge_points.practice: Given an editor sidebar and a file path, say which folder holds the file.

topics.title: Running code from the editor
topics.summary: Run the current file with the editor's Run button, find its output and errors in the output panel or integrated terminal, and avoid running the wrong file.

knowledge_points.title: The Run button and the output panel
knowledge_points.worked_example: Click Run (or press the shortcut) and the editor runs python3 on the open file; output appears in the panel below.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what appears in the output panel for a given file.

knowledge_points.title: Errors appear in the same panel
knowledge_points.worked_example: A traceback in the panel names the file and line; the program stopped there.
knowledge_points.practice: Read an editor error panel and give the file and line to fix.

knowledge_points.title: Run runs the active file
knowledge_points.worked_example: With test.py focused, Run runs test.py even if you were editing hello.py a moment ago.
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose 'my change did nothing' scenarios caused by the wrong active file or an unsaved file.

topics.title: Using editor feedback: colours, squiggles, line numbers
topics.summary: Use syntax highlighting, error underlines and line numbers to find mistakes before and after running, and toggle comments with a shortcut.

knowledge_points.title: Syntax colours reveal an unclosed string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hello)
print("Bye")
When the rest of the file turns string-coloured, a quote is missing.
knowledge_points.practice: Given highlighted code, locate the missing quote or parenthesis.

knowledge_points.title: Red underlines and the Problems list
knowledge_points.worked_example: Pylance/PyCharm underline Print("hi") with "Print is not defined" before you run anything.
knowledge_points.practice: Match underline messages to the line that causes them; fix the flagged lines.

knowledge_points.title: Jump to the line in an error message
knowledge_points.worked_example: Error says line 14: use Go to Line (Ctrl+G) or the line-number gutter to land on it.
knowledge_points.practice: Given an error message and numbered code, identify the faulty line.

knowledge_points.title: Toggle comments with a shortcut
knowledge_points.worked_example: Select lines and press Ctrl+/ (Cmd+/ on macOS): each line gets or loses a leading #.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output after toggling comments on selected lines.

topics.title: Code layout style: spaces, line length and comments
topics.summary: Apply PEP 8 layout rules to the code written so far: spacing in calls and keyword arguments, inline-comment spacing, and line length.

knowledge_points.title: Space after commas, none inside or before the parentheses
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print ( "a","b" )   # cramped and padded
print("a", "b")     # PEP 8
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the PEP 8 version of each line; fix spacing in a short program.

knowledge_points.title: No spaces around = in keyword arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a", "b", sep = "-")   # not PEP 8
print("a", "b", sep="-")     # PEP 8
knowledge_points.practice: Fix keyword-argument spacing; spot the one correctly styled line.

knowledge_points.title: Inline comments: two spaces before #, one after
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hi")  # greet
print("Hi") #greet   # not PEP 8
knowledge_points.practice: Fix comment spacing in several lines.

knowledge_points.title: Keep lines to 79 characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Long print calls can break inside the parentheses:
print("first part",
      "second part")
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which lines exceed the limit; rewrap a long print call so it still runs.

topics.title: Linters and formatters
topics.summary: Read a style checker's message (file:line:column code), fix what it flags, and let a formatter fix layout automatically, knowing style warnings don't stop a program.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a linter message
knowledge_points.worked_example:
hello.py:3:12: E231 missing whitespace after ','
File, line 3, column 12, rule E231, description.
knowledge_points.practice: Extract file, line and problem from linter output; fix the indicated line.

knowledge_points.title: A formatter rewrites layout for you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Before: print( "a","b" )
After running ruff format: print("a", "b")
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the formatter's output for badly spaced lines.

knowledge_points.title: Style warnings vs errors
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a","b")  runs fine and prints a b; the linter only complains about style.
print("a" "b"  is a SyntaxError and never runs.
knowledge_points.practice: For each flagged line decide whether the program still runs and what it prints.

topics.title: What a computer does when it runs a program
topics.summary: Name the CPU, main memory, secondary storage and input/output devices, say which keeps data after power-off, and order the steps by which Python source code gets run.

knowledge_points.title: The four parts
knowledge_points.worked_example: CPU: does the work. Main memory (RAM): fast, temporary. Secondary storage (SSD/disk): slow, permanent. Input/output: keyboard, screen, network.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify devices and descriptions into the four parts.

knowledge_points.title: What survives a power cut
knowledge_points.worked_example: Your open, unsaved hello.py lives in RAM and is lost on power-off; the saved file on disk survives.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide for each scenario whether the data survives; explain why saving matters.

knowledge_points.title: From file to running program
knowledge_points.worked_example: 1. hello.py sits on disk. 2. python3 loads it into memory. 3. The CPU executes the instructions. 4. Output goes to the screen.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of running a program (Parsons).

knowledge_points.title: Interpreters translate source code
knowledge_points.worked_example: The CPU only understands machine code. Python is an interpreter: it reads your source code and carries it out step by step.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose correct statements about source code, machine code, interpreters and compilers.
